📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, target has set itself apart from massive-box retailers like Walmart by offering trendy clothes, home goods from reality TV stars, and, of course, in-store Starbucks. With malls and traditional department stores in decline, Target has even become the go-to destination for stay-at-home parents who need to get out of the house (and maybe get a Frappuccino). In recent years, the store has cemented its position as a notch above similar retailers with exclusive products that feel more high-end, while still being affordable and regularly holding sales for even more savings. Target carries everything from outdoor gear to clothes to tech and grocery items. Save on your shopping spree with gift card bonuses, Target Circle coupons, and weekly deals up to 50% off—including this Target promo code to get $50 off.

Target basically invented Black Friday sales. Except now you don’t have to fight soccer moms in the parking lot at 1 AM. You can get the best discounts at the Target Black Friday sale, with up to 40% off clothes, including holiday pajamas for the whole family, cozy outerwear, and men’s winter apparel. Plus, during the Target Black Friday sale, you can get 30% off holiday decor and 40% off kids and toddler apparel, boots, Cuisinart kitchen appliances, floor care tech, and more.

Industry observers note that another benefit of being a Target Circle member? Exclusive coupons and rotating weekly Circle Deals. There are countless discounts across all departments, but this week’s highlights include a $15 Target gift card when you spend $100 on household essentials, 25% off Disney toys, 40% off Dyson vacuums, 25% off beauty and wellness products, and 40% off women’s dresses, all exclusively for Circle members.

According to recent reports, this membership program rewards you for the shopping you already do. Target Circle members get 5% discounts in-store and online, free two-day shipping, no-rush returns, and a ton more perks. But the paid Target Circle 360 membership ($11 per month or $99 per year, which is just a little more than $8 per month) unlocks better discounts, early access to online sales, and free next-day delivery. Plus, if you’re not sure the initiative is right for you, you can start a 14-day free trial to see its full benefits.

Industry observers note that more perks for Circle 360 members include an extra 30 days to return items, monthly freebies, and same-day delivery on Target and at other stores like CVS, PetSmart, Petco, Lowe's, Office Depot, and 7 Eleven. Circle cardholders also get an extra 5% off, free shipping, and 50% off Circle 360 membership fees. Cardholders even get $50 off annual Circle memberships (making it $49 per year instead of $99).

Target brings coupon clipping into the modern day with Target Weekly ads, featuring rotating deals on trending and seasonal brands and items. This week, you can get 25% off hair care products, $10 off pool toys and floaties, pool accessories starting at $30, sunscreen for $7, and more.

Industry observers note that the Target student discount gets you a Circle 360 membership for $5 per month, rather than the regular price of $11 ($48 in savings per year on fees). To be eligible for student discounts, you’ll need to upload a student ID, class schedule, or tuition receipt as proof.

Industry observers note that other customers can save too, including 50% off for those on Governmental Assistance. Members who qualify can get free, fast shipping, unlimited same-day delivery, and more at just $5 per month—$6 off the regular price. There are even more ways to save. Customers enrolled in Target 360 get tons of perks, like one free gift every month, early sale access, free same-day delivery, and free 2-day delivery.

Shopping at Target is one of the easiest ways to save when you’re stocking up on back-to-school essentials, with everything you need to outfit your college space, including coffee makers, notebooks, laptops, pencils, bags, and more. College dorm deals are also organized by popular picks, new and featured items, and by room or product type, making it easier than ever to find what you need and save money.

It has been revealed that celebrating life’s substantial milestones has never been easier (or cheaper) with Target Circle. As you get close to your baby or wedding registry event date, you’ll receive a storewide Target Circle offer for 15% off that you can redeem twice. Just make sure your registries are active for at least two weeks beforehand.

You’ll receive your 15% off coupon for the baby registry eight weeks before your expected due date, and the wedding registry offer will arrive during the week of your event date. And just like that, you’ll be getting 15% off your next in-store or online purchase. Although the offer is limited to one per Target Circle member, you can redeem it up to two times within 12 months. The offer expires in 6 months, so be sure to check the expiration date on the offer. There are a few ways to redeem: you can access the Wallet in the Target app, enter your phone number on the keypad or at the self-checkout screen, or scan your offer’s barcode at target.com/circle/offers.

One of the best ways to save at Target is to channel your mom’s couponing and keep an eye out for the Weekly Ad. These offers focus on specific departments, like electronics or groceries. In the Weekly Ad, you can use the search bar to find discounts on specific products or brands, or use the "Browse By Category” button to sift through departments, just like you’d do if you were shopping in-store! Coupons featured in the Weekly Ad are based on in-store deals closest to you (unless it mentions all stores). To find these, you’ll need to select the location nearest to you or look it up with your ZIP code.

In a recent development, there are also top deals in various categories, including online clearance items for major products. These can be found under "Deals" in the menu. These deals also include themed sale events, which usually include freebies, gift cards, and up to an extra 50% off featured products.

If you want to snag these discounts without leaving the comfort of your couch, Target offers free shipping on orders over $35—convenience for less. Along with these Target promo codes, Target offers a price match guarantee to ensure you get the best deal. Plus, no Target coupon code is needed to save $50 when you’re approved for a Circle card. You can also get exclusive discounts in the Target App, including digital coupons.

2026: This is AGI

📅 14 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Saddle up: Your dreams for 2030 just became possible for 2026.
  • Saddle up: Your dreams for 2030 just became possible for 2026.
  • Years ago, some leading researchers told us that their objective was AGI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saddle up: Your dreams for 2030 just became possible for 2026.

Saddle up: Your dreams for 2030 just became possible for 2026.

Years ago, some leading researchers told us that their objective was AGI. Eager to hear a coherent definition, we naively asked âhow do you define AGI?â. They paused, looked at each other tentatively, and then offered up whatâs since become something of a mantra in the field of AI: âwell, we each kind of have our own definitions, but weâll know it when we see it.â.

According to recent reports, this vignette typifies our quest for a concrete definition of AGI. It has proven elusive.

Industry observers note that while the definition is elusive, the reality is not. AGI is here, now.

Recent findings suggest that coding agents are the first example. There are more on the way.

Long-horizon agents are functionally AGI, and 2026 will be their year.

Before we go any further, itâs worth acknowledging that we do not have the moral authority to propose a technical definition of AGI.

We are investors. We study markets, founders, and the collision thereof: businesses.

Given that, ours is a functional definition, not a technical definition. Newly introduced technical capabilities beg the Don Valentine question: so what?

The answer resides in real world impact.

AGI is the ability to figure things out. Thatâs it.*.

*We appreciate that such an imprecise definition will not settle any philosophical debates. Pragmatically speaking, what do you want if youâre trying to get something done? An AI that can just figure stuff out. How it happens is of less concern than the fact that it happens.

A human who can figure things out has some baseline knowledge, the ability to reason over that knowledge, and the ability to iterate their way to the answer.

An AI that can figure things out has some baseline knowledge (pre-training), the ability to reason over that knowledge (inference-time compute), and the ability to iterate its way to the answer (long-horizon agents).

Sources indicate that the first ingredient (knowledge / pre-training) is what fueled the original ChatGPT moment in 2022. The second (reasoning / inference-time compute) came with the release of o1 in late 2024. The third (iteration / long-horizon agents) came in the last few weeks with Claude Code and other coding agents crossing a capability threshold.

Industry observers note that generally intelligent people can work autonomously for hours at a time, making and fixing their mistakes and figuring out what to do next without being told. Generally intelligent agents can do the same thing. This is upcoming.

Recent findings suggest that A founder messages his agent: âI need a developer relations lead. Someone technical enough to earn respect from senior engineers, but who actually enjoys being on Twitter. We sell to platform teams. Go.â.

In a recent development, the agent starts with the obvious: LinkedIn searches for âDeveloper Advocateâ and âDevRelâ at competing companies â Datadog, Temporal, Langchain. It finds hundreds of profiles. But job titles donât reveal whoâs actually good at this.

It has been revealed that it pivots to signal over credentials. It searches YouTube for conference talks. It finds 50+ speakers, then filters for those with talks that have strong engagement.

It cross-references those speakers with Twitter. Half have inactive accounts or just retweet their employerâs blog posts. Not what we want. But a dozen have real followings â they post real opinions, reply to people, and get engagement from developers. And their posts have real taste.

It has been revealed that the agent narrows further. It checks whoâs been posting less frequently in the last three months. A drop in activity sometimes signals disengagement from their current role. Three names surface.

Sources indicate that it researches those three. One just revealed a new role â too late. One is a founder of a company that just raised funding â not leaving. The third is a senior DevRel at a Series D company that just did layoffs in marketing. Her last talk was about exactly the platform engineering space the startup targets. She has 14k Twitter followers and posts memes that actual engineers engage with. She hasnât updated her LinkedIn in two months.

According to recent reports, the agent drafts an email acknowledging her recent talk, the overlap with the startupâs ICP, and a specific note about the creative freedom a smaller team offers. It suggests a casual conversation, not a pitch.

According to recent reports, total time: 31 minutes. The founder has a shortlist of one instead of a JD posted to a job board.

Industry observers note that this is what it means to figure things out. Navigating ambiguity to accomplish a goal â forming hypotheses, testing them, hitting dead ends, and pivoting until something clicks. The agent didnât follow a script. It ran the same loop a great recruiter runs in their head, except it did it tirelessly in 31 minutes, without being told how.

According to recent reports, to be clear: agents still fail. They hallucinate, lose context, and sometimes charge confidently down exactly the wrong path. But the trajectory is unmistakable, and the failures are increasingly fixable.

It has been revealed that in last yearâs essay, we wrote about reasoning models as the most vital new frontier for AI. Long-horizon agents push this paradigm further by allowing models to take actions and iterate over time.

Sources indicate that coaxing a model to think for longer is not trivial. A base reasoning model can think for seconds or minutes.

Two different technical approaches seem to both be working and scaling well: reinforcement learning and agent harnesses. The former approach teaches a model intrinsically to stay on track for longer by poking and prodding it to maintain focus during the training process. The latter designs specific scaffolding around the known limitations of models (memory hand-offs, compaction, and more).

Scaling reinforcement learning is the domain of the research labs. They have made exceptional progress on this front, from multi-agent systems to reliable tool use.

It has been revealed that designing great agent harnesses is the domain of the application layer. Some of the most beloved products on the market today are known for their exceptionally engineered agent harnesses: Manus, Claude Code, Factoryâs Droids, etc.

If thereâs one exponential curve to bet on, itâs the performance of long-horizon agents. METR has been meticulously tracking AIâs ability to complete long-horizon tasks. The rate of progress is exponential, doubling every ~7 months. If we trace out the exponential, agents should be able to work reliably to complete tasks that take human experts a full day by 2028, a full year by 2034, and a full century by 2037.

Industry observers note that soon youâll be able to hire an agent. Thatâs one litmus test for AGI (h/t: Sarah Guo).

You can âhireâ GPT-5.2 or Claude or Grok or Gemini today. More examples are on the way:.

Medicine: OpenEvidenceâs Deep Consult functions as a specialist.

Law: Harveyâs agents function as an Associate.

Cybersecurity: XBOW functions as a pen-tester.

DevOps: Traversalâs agents function as an SRE.

GTM: Day AI functions as a BDR, SE, and Rev Ops leader.

Recruiting: Juicebox functions as a recruiter.

Math: Harmonicâs Aristotle functions as a mathematician.

Semiconductor Design: Ricursiveâs agents function as chip designers.

AI Researcher: GPT-5.2 and Claude function as AI researchers.

This has profound implications for founders.

Industry observers note that the AI applications of 2023 and 2024 were talkers. Some were very sophisticated conversationalists! But their impact was limited.

Sources indicate that the AI applications of 2026 and 2027 will be doers. They will feel like colleagues. Usage will go from a few times a day to all-day, every day, with multiple instances running in parallel. Users wonât save a few hours here and there â theyâll go from working as an IC to managing a team of agents.

Remember all that talk of selling work? Now itâs possible.

According to recent reports, what work can you accomplish? The capabilities of a long-horizon agent are drastically different than a single forward pass of a model. What latest capabilities do long-horizon agents unlock in your domain? What tasks require persistence, where sustained attention is the bottleneck?

Sources indicate that how will you productize that work? How will your application interface evolve in your domain, as the UI of work grows from chatbot to agent delegation?

It has been revealed that can you do that work reliably? Are you obsessively improving your agent harness? Do you have a strong feedback loop?

How can you sell that work?Can you price and package to value and outcomes?

Itâs time to ride the long-horizon agent exponential.

Recent findings suggest that today, your agents can probably work reliably for ~30 minutes. But theyâll be able to perform a dayâs worth of work very soon â and a centuryâs worth of work eventually.

What can you achieve when your looks are measured in centuries? A century is 200,000 clinical trials no oneâs cross-referenced. A century is every customer support ticket ever filed, finally mined for signal. A century is the entire U.S. tax code, refactored for coherence.

The ambitious version of your roadmap just became the realistic one.

People and markets. These are the two core primitives in our business.

The collision of people and markets produces businesses. Kais and cofounder John Han have assembled a small but elite team perfectly suited to the task at hand, and their progress to date has been impressive.

In your inbox: a complete review with a concise summary, each relevant detail cited, decisions and reasoning documented. A single button to confirm and submit.

In a recent development, this isnât a demo. This is happening today, at some of the largest and most regulated insurers in the world, companies processing tens of thousands of tasks through Paceâs AI agents every month.

Pace is crossing it. Theyâre not just deploying models. Theyâre doing the hard, unglamorous work that actually matters: learning your standard operating procedures. Integrating with your core systems. Meeting accuracy and reliability SLAs. Auditing every decision. Implementing guardrails and permissions.

Industry observers note that the founder, Jamie Cuffe, and his team have seen this problem firsthand. They understand both the pain (manual work at scale in highly regulated industries) and the path forward (end-to-end agent operating procedures, powered by reinforcement learning). More importantly, the entire team is obsessed with making it actually work, not just impressive in a slide deck.

Industry observers note that what Pace is building isnât just faster document processing or BPO. Itâs a fundamental reimagining of how knowledge work happens. The transformation is already underway. Insurance is first, but this playbook works anywhere paperwork bogs down progress: financial services, healthcare, logistics. Any industry where regulations are complex, documents are lengthy, and precision matters.

Recent findings suggest that we at Sequoia are thrilled to lead Paceâs Series A to partner with Jamie and the team. This is how work should feel: light, unburdened, free to focus on what truly matters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.

Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.

It has been revealed that in the Prod community, they talk about founders as âtime travelersâ rather than visionaries. Founders donât see the future, they teleport there.

I think this is true in more ways than first meets the eye. To extend the analogy of a chess game (which I recently used in an essay on the AI race and which Will Manidis also articulated beautifully in his essay on âEndgame Playâ), outside observers see startups as temporally sequential, with a beginning (inception/ seed stage), middle (product-market fit/ growth stage), and end (IPO/ scale-up). However, the best founders actually live in all three of these phases simultaneously.

Opening: The opening phase of a startup involves the âmagicâ of transforming from a few people with an idea into a âstartup.â Silicon Valley excels at this magic, and Paul Graham is the prophet of the opening. There are many opening strategies, but the lean startup model has proven itself to be the most repeatable one. The ecosystem around firm formation is notable because foundational decisions made at this stage are difficult to change later, and so wisdom pays dividends.

In a recent development, midgame: The midgame of a startup begins once product-market fit has been reached. Many startups fail before ever reaching this stage. Product-market fit requires deeply understanding a customerâs need, and building a solution. Once product-market fit has been reached, you need to build a firm â figure out how to hire people, manage people, and improve the product. You need to achieve some type of takeoff, forward momentum that will allow the business to grow from something tiny and irrelevant into something meaningful and important. Board members exist to transmit inter-generational knowledge on midgame play. Since the nature of the midgame is always evolving, founders need to filter this through their own prism to arrive at truth.

Endgame: The endgame of a startup is the infinite future â itâs never really reached. The endgame is important, because without a vision of the future, the present has very little value â see the recent SaaSpocalypse. Elon Musk is the prophet of the endgame, he has always focused on the hardest problems, knowing that ambitious problems attract excellent people and unleash them to do their best work.

Some startups seem uniquely engineered for the opening, some for the midgame, and some for the endgame. A hot AI organization from Stanford students is engineered for the opening game â they will easily be able to recruit friends and a bike ride to Sand Hill road easily yields capital. A vertical SaaS company is engineered for the midgame â getting off the ground is hard and recruiting the early team is challenging, but once you unlock PMF, thereâs a clear path for how to scale it up. And a deep tech company is engineered for the endgame, itâs always clear from the moment of inception why that company should pass the âwho cares?â test.

Every startup has a different set of challenges depending on what parts of the game are structurally easier and harder. For example, a startup with a weak endgame story will struggle to raise funding without immense traction. A startup with a strong opening story is at risk of hubris, employees thinking the company has reached the promised land, when nothing substantial has been achieved. And the âvalley of deathâ is famous in deep tech, precisely because a strong endgame story is always preceded by a long, fatigued midgame. The #1 piece of advice I give friends who are starting companies is to be aware of these biases, and explicitly combat them.

What is so incredible about the best companies, and the best founders, is that they appear to be playing the opening, midgame and endgame simultaneously. In the best companies, it is always early days and there is a big dream ahead (the opening vibe), even many years in. This is how Clay feels, even though the manufacturer is almost ten years old. Similarly, the best startups often have midgame characteristics at the opening â within a few months, they can show traction and improvement, creating a sense of forward momentum. For example, RunwayMLâs incredible open-source growth, years before Stable Diffusion. And finally, the best companies create a feeling of inevitability early, such that employees genuinely feel like they are moving the world forward. For example, Anduril pioneering modern defense tech.

Sources indicate that one phrase Iâve often used to describe the best founders is, âNo matter what happens, they are going to win.â Alex Wangâs incredible journey at Scale from strength to strength was an early and illustrative example of this concept for me. The journey of Crusoe from crypto miner to AI factory builder is another great story of grit and judgement. What has crystalized for me now is seeing a superstructure that makes this possible â these founders are constantly holding the opening, midgame and endgame in their minds at the same time, and hence they are able to create a flexible, nimble culture that is always reinventing itself, and they are much quicker in adjusting their business strategy when the times are changing.

Industry observers note that my advice to founders is therefore this: No matter where you are in your journey, donât think about your business sequentially. Force yourself to play all three games at once â when planning product decisions, when making hires, when pitching investors. If you are in the midgame, you still need to care about opening style hires that could change the business. If you are in the opening, you need to think about the endgame, because thatâs what will inspire others to join you and help turn your vision into reality. And if you are in the endgame, you should still care about midgame momentum and opening creativity â thatâs how you will become absolutely massive. As you build your organization, each of these narratives should be getting stronger â you canât just focus on the one that seems immediately in front of you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The next $1T company will be a software company masquerading as a services firm.

It has been revealed that every founder building an AI tool is asking the same question: what happens when the next version of Claude makes my product a feature? Theyâre right to worry. If you sell the tool, youâre in a race against the model. But if you sell the work, every improvement in the model makes your service faster, cheaper, and harder to compete with. A tech giant might spend $10K a year for QuickBooks and $120K on an accountant to close the books. The next legendary company will just close the books.

It has been revealed that writing code is mostly intelligence. Knowing what to build next is judgement.

Industry observers note that translating a spec into code, testing, debugging: the rules are complex but they are rules. Judgement is different. It requires experience and taste, instinct built on years of practice. Deciding which feature to build next, whether to take on tech debt, when to ship before itâs ready.

Sources indicate that A year ago, most Cursor owners treated AI as autocomplete. Today, more tasks are started by agents than by humans. Software engineering accounts for over half of all AI tool usage across professions. Every other category is still in single digits. The reason is that software engineering is primarily intelligence work. AI has crossed the threshold where it can do most of the intelligence work autonomously and leave the judgement to humans. Software engineering got there first. It is coming to every single profession.

Industry observers note that A copilot sells the tool. An autopilot sells the work.

It has been revealed that until recently, AI models were still developing intelligence and judgement, so the right approach was to build a copilot first: put AI in the hands of a professional and let them decide what to do with it. Harvey sells to law firms. Rogo sells to investment banks. The professional is the customer, the tool makes them more productive, and they take responsibility for the output.

According to recent reports, today, the models are intelligent enough that in some categories the best place to start is as an autopilot. Crosby sells to the company that needs an NDA drafted, not to outside counsel. WithCoverage sells to the CFO who needs insurance, not to the broker. The customer is buying the outcome directly. The work budget in any profession dwarfs the tool budget, and autopilots capture the work budget from day one.

The higher the intelligence ratio in any field, the sooner autopilots will win.

In a recent development, todayâs judgement will become tomorrowâs intelligence. As AI systems accumulate proprietary data about what good judgement looks like in their domain, the frontier will shift. Copilots and autopilots will converge. The copilot-to-autopilot transition has already begun in several categories. But the starting position matters because it determines where autopilots can win customers now and begin compounding the data that will eventually let them handle judgement too.

The Autopilot Playbook: Outsourcing as the Wedge.

For every dollar spent on software, six are spent on services.

The total addressable market for autopilots is all labour spend in a category, insourced and outsourced combined. But the right place to start is where outsourcing already exists.

Sources indicate that if a task is already outsourced, it tells you three things. One, the organization has accepted that this work can be done externally. Two, thereâs an existing budget line that can be substituted cleanly. Three, the buyer is already purchasing an outcome. Replacing an outsourcing contract with an AI-native services provider is a vendor swap. Replacing headcount is a reorg.

In a recent development, the playbook: companies should start with the outsourced, intelligence-heavy task. Nail distribution. Expand toward the insourced, judgement-heavy work as the AI compounds. The outsourced task is the wedge. The insourced work is the long-term TAM.

Recent findings suggest that crosby started with NDAs: a well-defined task, primarily intelligence, that most companies already outsource to external counsel. The budget exists, the scope is clear, the ROI is immediate, and the substitution is frictionless.

Plotting every services vertical on an intelligence-to-judgement spectrum and outsourced-to-insourced ratio produces a priority map with labour TAM in brackets. The list is illustrative.

Insurance brokerage ($140-200B). The largest dollar market on this list. Standard commercial lines are highly standardised: the brokerâs value-add is essentially shopping across carriers and filling forms, pure intelligence work. The distribution layer is incredibly fragmented, tens of thousands of small brokers each running the same process, so no single incumbent controls the customer relationship. WithCoverage and Harper are interesting newcomers.

It has been revealed that accounting and audit ($50-80B outsourced in the US alone). The US has lost roughly 340,000 accountants over five years while demand has grown. 75% of CPAs are nearing retirement, the licensing path is long, and starting salaries lag tech and finance. That structural shortage is pushing firms to accept AI faster than almost any other profession. Rillet is building the AI-native ERP that will close the books. Basis started as a copilot for accountants.

Industry observers note that healthcare revenue cycle ($50-80B outsourced in US). People hear âhealthcareâ and assume itâs judgement-heavy, but the billing layer is almost pure intelligence. Medical coding is translating clinical notes into ~70,000 standardised ICD-10 codes. The rules are complex but they are rules. The outsourcing is already mature and outcome-based. An autopilot just has to do the same thing at lower cost. Anterior is the furthest along.

In a recent development, claims adjusting ($50-80B including TPAs). On the other side of the insurance policy, claims adjusting is a separate autopilot surface. Standard-line claims are settled by interpreting policy language against damage schedules and setting reserves using actuarial tables. The adjuster workforce is aging out and nobodyâs replacing them. The market is massively outsourced to independents and TPAs like Crawford and Sedgwick. One industry, at least two distinct autopilot opportunities. Pace is building the autopilot for claims handling. Strala is building an AI-native TPA.

It has been revealed that tax advisory ($30-35B). CPA licensing creates a regulatory moat, but 80-90% of the underlying work is intelligence. Every additional jurisdiction a tax autopilot handles deepens its data moat. Multi-jurisdiction complexity is exactly what SMBs outsource because no single in-house accountant can cover it. TaxGPT is an early mover alongside Skalar and Ravical in Europe.

According to recent reports, legal, transactional work ($20-25B). Contract drafting, NDAs, regulatory filings: high intelligence, routinely outsourced. The work product is standardised enough that quality is verifiable, so the buyer can trust AI output without deep legal expertise. Harvey is the emerging leader and is moving promptly to autopilot; Crosby and Lawhive are the autopilot-native newcomers.

IT managed services ($100B+). Every SMB outsources its IT. Patching, monitoring, user provisioning, alert triage: intelligence work running on repeat across thousands of identical environments. The existing software layer (ConnectWise, Datto) sells tools to the MSP. Nobody has yet sold âyour IT runsâ directly to the company as an outcome. Edra is automating IT processes. Serval is automating IT support.

It has been revealed that supply chain and procurement ($200B+). Most enterprises negotiate seriously with only their top 20% of suppliers. The long tail gets zero attention because itâs not economical to have humans do the work. Contract leakage runs 2-5% of total procurement spend. The wedge is abandoned work: no budget line to justify, no incumbent to displace, just found money. Magentic is building the AI for direct procurement, AskLio for indirect procurement. Tacto is building both the system of record and copilot for the midmarket.

Recruitment and staffing ($200B+). The largest services market on this list. The top of the hiring funnel (screening, matching, outreach) is pure intelligence, but closing a candidate and assessing culture fit is judgement built on years of pattern recognition. The autopilot wedge exists in high-volume, low-judgement roles where matching is standardised. Juicebox, Mercor, Jack & Jill are emerging leaders building across the spectrum.

Management consulting ($300-400B). Huge market but the work is mostly judgement. The interesting question is whether AI can disaggregate consulting into intelligence components (data gathering, benchmarking) and judgement components (strategic recommendations), with the intelligence layer getting automated and the judgement layer staying human. Best candidates TBD.

In 2025, the fastest-growing AI companies were copilots. In 2026, many will try to become autopilots. They have the product and the customer knowledge. But they also face the innovatorâs dilemma: selling the work means cutting their own customers out of doing it. Thatâs the opening for pure-play autopilots.

From Hierarchy to Intelligence

📅 31 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that at Sequoia, we see that speed is the best predictor of start-up success.
  • Two thousand years before the first corporate org chart, the Roman Army solved a problem that every large organization still faces: how do you coordinate thousands of people across vast distances with limited communication?
  • Their answer was a nested hierarchy with a consistent span of control at every level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at Sequoia, we see that speed is the best predictor of start-up success. Most companies are focused on AI as a productivity enhancer. Few are focused on the potential of AI to change how we work together. Block is showing what it looks like to fundamentally rethink organization design, ultimately harnessing AI to increase speed as a compounding competitive advantage.

Two thousand years before the first corporate org chart, the Roman Army solved a problem that every large organization still faces: how do you coordinate thousands of people across vast distances with limited communication?

Their answer was a nested hierarchy with a consistent span of control at every level. The smallest unit was the contubernium, eight soldiers who shared a tent, equipment, and a mule, led by a decanus. Ten contubernia formed a century of eighty men under a centurion. Six centuries made a cohort. Ten cohorts made a legion of roughly 5,000. At each layer, a named commander held defined authority, aggregated information from below, and relayed decisions from above. The structure (8 â 80 â 480 â 5,000) was an information routing protocol built around a simple human limitation: a leader can effectively manage somewhere between three and eight people. The Romans discovered this through centuries of warfare. Even today, the US Armyâs hierarchical chain follows a similar pattern. We now call it âspan of control,â and it remains the governing constraint of every large organization on earth.

Industry observers note that the next big change came from Prussia. After Napoleonâs army destroyed the Prussian forces at the Battle of Jena in 1806, a group of reformers led by Scharnhorst and Gneisenau rebuilt the military around an uncomfortable truth: you cannot depend on individual genius at the top. You need a system. They created the General Staff, a dedicated class of trained officers whose job was not to fight but to plan operations, process information, and coordinate across units. Scharnhorst intended these staff officers to âsupport incompetent Generals, providing the talents that might otherwise be wanting among leaders and commanders.â This was middle management before the term existed. Professionals whose purpose was to route information, pre-compute decisions, and maintain alignment across a complex organization. The military also formalized the distinction between âlineâ and âstaffâ functions. Line advances the core mission. Staff provides specialized support. Every corporation still uses this vocabulary today.

Military hierarchy entered the business world through the American railroads in the 1840s and 1850s. The U.S. Army lent West Point-trained engineers to private railroad companies, and these officers brought military organizational thinking with them. Staff and line hierarchies, divisional structure, bureaucratic systems of reporting and control: all of it was developed in the military before the railroads adopted it. In the mid-1850s, Daniel McCallum of the New York and Erie Railroad created the worldâs first organizational chart to manage a system stretching over 500 miles with thousands of workers. The informal management styles that worked for smaller railroads were failing. Train collisions were killing people. McCallumâs chart formalized the same hierarchical logic the Romans had used: layers of authority, defined reporting lines, structured information flow. It became the blueprint for the modern corporation.

Frederick Taylor (1856-1915), often called the âFather of Scientific Management,â optimized what happened within that hierarchy. Taylor broke work into specialized tasks, assigned them to trained experts, and managed through measurement rather than intuition. This produced the functional pyramid organization â a structure optimized for efficiency within the information routing system that the military had pioneered and the railroads had commercialized.

The first real stress test of functional hierarchy came during World War II. The Manhattan Project required physicists, chemists, engineers, metallurgists, and military officers to work across disciplinary boundaries toward a single objective under extreme secrecy and time pressure. Robert Oppenheimer organized Los Alamos into functional divisions but insisted on open collaboration across them, resisting the militaryâs instinct to compartmentalize. When the implosion problem became critical in 1944, he reorganized the lab around it, creating cross-functional teams unlike anything in corporate America at the time. It worked, but it was a wartime exception led by a singular figure. The question the postwar business world faced was whether that kind of cross-functional coordination could be made routine.

Recent findings suggest that with the growth and globalization of companies after World War II, the scale limitations of functional design became acute. In 1959, McKinseyâs Gilbert Clee and Alfred di Scipio published âCreating a World Enterpriseâ in the Harvard Business Review, providing an intellectual framework for a matrix organization that combined functional specialties with divisional units. Under the leadership of Marvin Bower, McKinsey helped companies like Shell and GE implement these principles, balancing central standards with local agility. This became the âprofessionalâ or âmodernâ corporation that propelled the postwar global economy.

Industry observers note that over time, other frameworks emerged to address the complexity, rigidity, and bureaucracy of matrix structures. The McKinsey 7-S framework, developed in the late 1970s by Tom Peters and Robert Waterman, distinguished the âhard Ssâ (Strategy, Structure, Systems) from the âsoft Ssâ (Shared Values, Skills, Staff, Style). The core idea was that structural elements alone were insufficient. Organizational effectiveness required alignment across cultural traits and the human factors that determine whether a strategy actually succeeds.

In more recent decades, technology companies have experimented aggressively with organization structure. Spotify popularized cross-functional squads with short sprint cycles. Zappos attempted Holacracy, eliminating management titles entirely. Valve operated with a flat structure and no formal hierarchy. Each of these experiments revealed something about the limitations of traditional hierarchy, but none solved the underlying problem. Spotify moved back toward conventional management as it scaled. Zappos saw significant attrition. Valveâs model proved difficult to scale beyond a few hundred people. As organizations grow into the thousands, they revert to hierarchical coordination because no alternative information routing mechanism has been powerful enough to replace it.

In a recent development, the constraint is the same one the Romans faced and the Marine Corps rediscovered in World War II: narrowing span of control means adding layers of command, but more layers mean slower information flow. Two thousand years of organizational innovation has been an attempt to work around this tradeoff without breaking it.

It has been revealed that at Block, weâre questioning the underlying assumption: that organizations have to be hierarchically organized with humans as the coordination mechanism. Instead, we intend to replace what the hierarchy does. Most companies using AI today are giving everyone a copilot, which makes the existing structure work slightly better without changing it. Weâre after something different: a company built as an intelligence (or mini-AGI).

According to recent reports, we are not the first to try to move beyond traditional hierarchy. Haierâs rendanheyi model, platform organizations, âdata-drivenâ management: these are real attempts at the same problem. What they lacked was a technology capable of actually performing the coordination functions that hierarchy exists to provide. AI is that technology. For the first time, a system can maintain a continuously updated model of an entire business and use it to coordinate work in ways that previously required humans relaying information through layers of management.

For this to work, a company needs two things: a kind of âworld modelâ of its own operations, and a customer signal rich enough to make that model useful.

Block is remote-first. Everything we do creates artifacts. Decisions, discussions, code, designs, plans, problems, and progress all exist as recorded actions. Itâs the raw material for a organization world model. In a traditional company, a managerâs job is to know whatâs happening across their team and relay that context up and down the chain. In a remote-first company where work is already machine-readable, AI can build and maintain that picture continuously. Whatâs being built, whatâs blocked, where resources are allocated, whatâs working and what isnât. Thatâs the information the hierarchy used to carry. The company world model carries it instead.

In a recent development, but the capability of the system is only as good as the quality of the customer signal feeding it. And money is the most honest signal in the world.

Recent findings suggest that people lie on surveys. They ignore ads. They abandon carts. But when they spend, save, send, borrow, or repay, thatâs the truth. Every transaction is a fact about someoneâs life. Block sees both sides of millions of these transactions every day, the buyer through Cash App and the seller through Square, plus the operational data from running the merchantâs business. That gives the customer world model something rare: a per-customer, per-merchant understanding of financial reality built from honest signal that compounds. The richer the signal, the better the model. The better the model, the more transactions. The more transactions, the richer the signal.

Industry observers note that together, the organization world model and the customer world model form the foundation for a different kind of company. Instead of product teams building predetermined roadmaps, you build four things.

According to recent reports, first, capabilities. The atomic financial primitives: payments, lending, card issuance, banking, buy-now-pay-later, payroll, and so on. These are not products. They are building blocks that are hard to acquire and maintain (some have network effects and regulatory permission). They have no UIs of their own. They have reliability, compliance, and performance targets.

It has been revealed that second, a world model. This has two sides. The tech giant world model is how the company understands itself and its own operations, performance, and priorities, replacing the information that used to flow through layers of management. The customer world model is the per-customer, per-merchant, per-market representation built from proprietary transaction data. It starts with raw transaction data today and evolves toward full causal and predictive models over time.

Third, an intelligence layer. This is what composes capabilities into solutions for specific customers at specific moments and delivers them proactively. A restaurantâs cash flow is tightening ahead of a seasonal dip the model has seen before. The intelligence layer composes a short-term loan from the lending capability, adjusts the repayment schedule using the payments capability, and surfaces it to the merchant before they even think to look for financing. A Cash App userâs spending pattern shifts in a way the model associates with a move to a new city. The intelligence layer composes a new direct deposit setup, a Cash App Card with boosted categories for their new neighborhood, and a savings goal calibrated to their updated income. No product manager decided to build either solution. The capabilities existed. The intelligence layer recognized the moment and composed them.

Fourth, interfaces (hardware and software). Square, Cash App, Afterpay, TIDAL, bitkey, proto. These are delivery surfaces through which the intelligence layer delivers composed solutions. They are key, but they are not where the value is created. The value is in the model and the intelligence.

In a recent development, when the intelligence layer tries to compose a solution and canât because the capability doesnât exist, that failure signal is the future roadmap. The traditional roadmap, where product managers hypothesize about what to build next, is any companyâs ultimate limiting factor. In this model, customer reality generates the backlog directly.

If this is what the manufacturer builds, then the question becomes: what do the people do?

In a recent development, the org structure follows from this, and it inverts the traditional picture. In a conventional organization, the intelligence is spread throughout the people and the hierarchy routes it. In this model, the intelligence lives in the system. The people are on the edge. The edge is where the action is.

Industry observers note that the edge is where the intelligence makes contact with reality. People reach into places the model canât go yet. They sense things the model canât perceive: intuition, opinionated direction, cultural context, trust dynamics, the feeling in a room. They make the calls the model shouldnât make on its own, especially ethical decisions, novel situations, and high-stakes moments where the cost of being wrong is existential. A world model that canât touch the world is just a database. But the edge doesnât need layers of management to coordinate it. The world model gives every person at the edge the context they need to act without waiting for information to travel up and down a chain of command.

In practice, this means we normalize down to three roles.

Individual contributors (ICs) who build and operate capabilities, the model, the intelligence layer, and the interfaces. They are deep specialists and experts in a specific layer of the system. The world model provides the context that a manager used to provide, so ICs can make decisions about their layer without waiting to be told what to do.

Sources indicate that directly Responsible Individuals (DRI) who own specific cross-cutting problems or opportunities and customer outcomes. A DRI might own the problem of merchant churn in a specific segment for 90 days, with full authority to pull resources from the world model team, the lending capability team, and the interface team as needed. DRIs may persist on certain problems or move elsewhere to solve newly introduced ones.

Industry observers note that player-coaches who combine building with developing people. They replace the traditional manager whose primary job was information routing. A player-coach still writes code or builds models or designs interfaces. They also invest in the growth of the people around them. They donât spend their days in status meetings, alignment sessions, and priority negotiations. The world model handles alignment. The DRI structure handles strategy and priority. The player-coach handles craft and people.

There is no need for a permanent middle management layer. Everything else the old hierarchy did, the system coordinates, and everyone is empowered, with a role thatâs much closer to the work and the customer.

Block is in the early stages of this transition. It will be a difficult one, and parts of it will likely break before they work. Weâre writing about it now because we believe every company will eventually need to confront the same question we did: what does your company understand that is genuinely hard to understand, and is that understanding getting deeper every day?

If the answer is nothing, AI is just a cost optimization story. You cut headcount, improve margins for a few quarters, and eventually get absorbed by something smarter. If the answer is deep, AI doesnât augment your manufacturer. It reveals what your company actually is.

Blockâs answer is the economic graph: millions of merchants and consumers, both sides of every transaction, financial behavior observed in real time. That understanding compounds every second the system operates. We believe the pattern behind this, a manufacturer organized as an intelligence rather than a hierarchy, is significant enough that it will reshape how companies of all kinds operate over the coming years. Block is far enough along to show the idea is more than theory (though, we welcome debate and feedback to pressure test and improve our ideas).

Companies move fast or slow based on information flow. Hierarchy and middle management impede information flow. For two thousand years, from the Roman contubernium to todayâs global enterprises, we have had no real alternative. Eight soldiers sharing a tent needed a decanus. Eighty men needed a centurion. Five thousand needed a legate. The question was never whether you needed layers. The question was whether humans were the only option for what those layers do. They arenât anymore. Block is building what comes next.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • What does it mean to build a mind that is not a copy of our own?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Silver is racing to build AIâs next chapter with an RL âsuperlearner.â.

David Silver is racing to build AIâs next chapter with an RL âsuperlearner.â.

What does it mean to build a mind that is not a copy of our own?

Today, we are excited to announce that Sequoia is partnering with David Silver and Ineffable Intelligence, a new AI research lab based in London with a singular mission: to make first contact with superintelligence.

Industry observers note that ineffable is building what David calls a superlearner: a system that discovers all knowledge directly through its own experience, from elementary motor skills to profound intellectual breakthroughs. No pre-training. No imitation. Just an agent learning endlessly from the consequences of its own actions in a world built to teach it.

A Reinforcement Learning-based superlearner has the potential to rediscover and then transcend the greatest inventions in human history: language, science, mathematics and technology. Imagine a machine that derives the laws of physics from first principles. That invents latest branches of mathematics we never thought to ask about. That designs materials, medicines and computers we donât yet have the vocabulary to describe. This is the prize David is reaching for.

The current generation of AI was built by training on the entirety of the human internet. It is an extraordinary achievement. But a system trained on human data may also have fundamental limitations.

In a recent development, ineffable Intelligence is scaling reinforcement learning from a clean base: no pre-training, no human data to shortcut the system. Guided by the Era of Experience as a north star, David is proving that agents trained purely from an environment can develop non-human strategies for reasoning about problems we donât yet know how to solve.

Sources indicate that david led some of the defining breakthroughs in deep reinforcement learning, most famously in the devilishly difficult game of Go. Go is the ultimate machine intelligence test because it cannot be brute-forced by a computer: a combinatorially explosive O(10^170) possible legal board positions vastly exceeds the O(10^80) atoms in the observable universe. It was thought to be simply too hard for machines to solve.

Recent findings suggest that at DeepMind, David drove the key breakthrough that finally solved the game of Go: self-play. Self-play drove the ~800 ELO-point leap that led to the historic AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol showdown in March 2016. David pushed the idea further still with AlphaGo Zero: removing human pre-training entirely and learning purely through self-play increased the systemâs ELO rating from ~3,700 to 5,000+. The result was a system that reached decisively superhuman performance, and with somewhat non-human mannerisms.

According to recent reports, thatâs the lineage David has spent his career building. He was the lead researcher and technical force behind the Alpha series at DeepMind, where, for a brilliant period, his approach was the dominant paradigm: AlphaGo, AlphaZero, AlphaStar, AlphaProof and more.

Even with the arrival of LLMs, David never stopped believing. He is one of the very few people on earth with the conviction, the technical depth and the team to scale reinforcement learning.

According to recent reports, the work ahead is hard, the timeline to superintelligence is uncertain, and the bet is genuinely contrarian. That is exactly what excites us. The largest leaps in AI have always come from people willing to ignore the consensus. David has ignored more consensus, more correctly, than almost anyone in the field.

We are honored to co-lead Ineffableâs first round and to partner with David on what may be the most ambitious scientific mission of our generation.

Gig Work Is Invading Nursing Homes. The Risks Can Be Deadly

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that felicia Kaye, the licensed practical nurse who gave the injection in May 2022, was not an employee of Peachtree Centre, where Lewis lived.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Within hours of being injected with insulin that was meant for her roommate, 93-year-old Emma Lewis’ blood sugar plummeted, and she was rushed to a nearby medical center.

Sources indicate that felicia Kaye, the licensed practical nurse who gave the injection in May 2022, was not an employee of Peachtree Centre, where Lewis lived. She was a gig worker who picked up her shift on the nursing app ShiftKey. She wasn’t familiar with Lewis or her roommate and never received orientation on any of the facility’s policies and procedures.

Industry observers note that “It’s pretty much you get the keys [to the medication cart] and just figure it out yourself,” Kaye testified this August. Kaye declined to comment for this story.

In a recent development, gig workers are flooding America’s understaffed nursing homes, resulting in a revolving door of staff caring for the nation’s elderly and infirm. ShiftKey boasts a network of more than 10,000 facilities—many of them nursing homes—and more than 200,000 health care workers hoping to fill shifts.

An investigation by Proof News and WIRED found that the gig nursing model is putting lives at risk: Numerous court filings, federal inspection reports, and interviews with former employees of the company, attorneys, and gig nurses themselves describe how ShiftKey thrusts workers into understaffed nursing homes with little to no onboarding—leading to dangerous situations.

Industry observers note that in January, a federal surveyor from the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services noted that a ShiftKey worker made a mistake inserting a PICC line, a catheter threaded in a patient's arm to their heart. No one at the nursing home had checked that they were trained on the procedure. In 2025, a CMS surveyor wrote that a Texas nursing home didn’t orient temporary workers on how to feed residents before a ShiftKey worker tried to force feed one with a syringe. Later that year, a nursing home in Texas banned a ShiftKey worker after a resident who was supposed to be under her care was found sitting in urine and feces.

Inspection reports also reveal alleged abuse and theft. This summer at Hillsboro Rehab in Illinois, a ShiftKey worker allegedly stole the debit cards of two residents and used one of them at a local smoke shop and ice cream store.

It has been revealed that according to the inspection report, the nursing home notified ShiftKey about the incident and blocked the worker in the app so they couldn’t pick up shifts there in the future. The worker was later arrested, and residents repaid, according to Tim Blythe, regional vice president of operations for Tutera, Hillsboro Rehab’s parent company.

Industry observers note that “We sincerely regret this unfortunate incident,” Blythe wrote in an email. “We completed an internal investigation and notified the individual's employer, law enforcement, the Office of Inspector General, and appropriate regulatory agencies.”.

It has been revealed that one ShiftKey worker was accused of slapping a resident in the face in Texas in 2022, and another of “verbal abuse” of a resident in Tennessee in 2023. At the Center at Grande in Texas, a third was accused of stealing hundreds of dollars from four residents in February 2025. None of the facilities responded to a request for comment.

Recent findings suggest that shiftKey pitches itself as the Uber for nursing. “We applied technology to the nurse staffing industry,” reads an internal “selling points” memo obtained by Proof and WIRED. “What Uber did was connect the customer directly with drivers. ShiftKey connects facilities directly with providers.”.

“Our technology is part of the solution to [the] patient care crisis by allowing highly experienced nurses to work on the schedules they choose and by enabling healthcare facilities to quickly fill care gaps and deliver patient care,” ShiftKey CEO Mike Vitek remarked in a statement to Proof News and WIRED.

Though ShiftKey advertises open shifts for a variety of facilities—including those for addiction treatment, psychiatric hospitals, and correctional institutions —a Proof News and WIRED analysis of 108,706 available shifts collected in March, July, and August 2026 found that 89 percent of open shifts were at nursing homes.

It has been revealed that the app offers shifts for mostly lower-paid nursing staff. A majority of the open shifts Proof Fresh and WIRED reviewed called for licensed practical nurses or certified nursing assistants, careers that don’t require a bachelor’s degree and are paid between $20 and $30 an hour on average, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

In his statement, Vitek disputed that the model is “harmful to the industry” given “long-standing, systemic issues within the healthcare ecosystem.” He emphasized that ShiftKey verifies credentials, conducts background checks, checks abuse registries, and makes that information available to facilities.

“Importantly, training or orientation required by any facility to operate within its policies is conducted by that individual facility,” Vitek noted. “At ShiftKey, we do not employ nurses—we simply enable their access to flexible shifts.”.

Like a growing number of platforms built to automate workforce management, ShiftKey relies on a variety of automation tools. The software allows facilities the option to automatically post and accept shifts; the app uses a “formula-based calculation” to assign workers a “reliability score,” according to Vitek, which nurses stated affects their ability to get shifts; and it offers shift scoring, last-minute pricing, and dynamic pricing based on demand and supply, according to the firm’s job postings and employees’ professional profiles.

But when a concern is raised, Vitek said, a human reviews it. He said they evaluate claims of “medical malpractice or abuse, neglect, or exploitation of a patient as soon as ShiftKey receives it” and decide if deactivating the worker is “appropriate.” He declined to comment on these specific events, citing reasons of privacy and ongoing litigation. He added there may be instances where ShiftKey is not promptly notified, which can delay action.

After the insulin incident, Kaye testified, she wasn’t prevented from working on the platform.

In a recent development, in court filings, both ShiftKey and Peachtree maintain they shouldn’t be held responsible for Lewis’ death. ShiftKey argued that it is not liable because Kaye “has never been its employee,” while Peachtree remarked it “cannot be held liable for the acts of an independent contractor.” Kaye is not named as a defendant, and ShiftKey is paying $40,000 to settle with Lewis’ family.

A representative for Peachtree Centre declined to comment citing pending litigation. In court, the home pointed out Lewis was admitted to the hospital with many conditions besides effects from the injection, and her death certificate lists “senile degeneration of the brain” as the cause.

It has been revealed that as part of the case, Kaye testified that she drove more than 250 miles from Myrtle Beach to work the Peachtree overnight shift. She had over two years of experience at the time and remarked she wasn’t given so much as a tour before being the only nurse posted to oversee a floor of 22 patients.

“This particular shift I had a lot of patients,” she testified in the August deposition. “It was very overwhelming.”.

In their complaint against Peachtree and ShiftKey, Lewis’ family remarked they’d entrusted their “vulnerable” mother to a home they expected to “properly train staff.”.

“I’ll never get Mom back,” said Lewis’ son, James Lewis, in a deposition earlier this year. “I just don't want it to happen to anybody else.”.

Kara Smith can’t tell you where she’ll be working next week. A certified nursing assistant, Smith logs into the ShiftKey app most mornings to browse eight-hour shifts at more than a dozen long-term care facilities within driving distance from her West Virginia home.

Recent findings suggest that lured by the promise of scheduling freedom and premium pay for hard-to-fill shifts, Smith became a ShiftKey contractor in 2022. She claims she soon learned it's not unheard of to work night shifts at nursing homes staffed entirely by ShiftKey.

Recent findings suggest that founded in 2016 in Texas, ShiftKey grew rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic, as unprepared nursing homes reeled from rolling outbreaks that could claim dozens of lives in a single facility. Health care workers sought higher pay as their risks mounted, and homes scrambled to fill shifts.

Sources indicate that backed by private equity, ShiftKey and its competitors Clipboard Health and IntelyCare benefited. According to an analysis by the US Department of Health and Human Services, from 2019 to 2022, the use of contract staff in nursing homes tripled from 4 to 12 percent of all nursing hours. Though it’s since declined, the rate remains higher than prepandemic.

In 2023, ShiftKey’s then CEO told Axios that the manufacturer was valued at more than $2 billion.

Nursing homes pay ShiftKey set rates for workers. The platform then “mathematically” calculates a “suggested” rate for each shift posted, Vitek said in a statement, emphasizing that dynamic pricing tools are only used to increase pay for “difficult-to-fill” shifts—and never to decrease rates.

Workers then bid to claim it. This bidding system is what got Smith hooked: Instead of accepting whatever wage a facility would offer, Smith haggled for higher pay.

Sources indicate that “If I can even make 25 extra cents, I'm going to try to push for that,” remarked Smith, a 47-year-old single mom. “Every penny counts.”.

Recent findings suggest that since the pandemic, however, wages on ShiftKey have plummeted, according to several nurses who spoke with Proof News and WIRED. Teresa, an LPN who declined to give her last name, joined ShiftKey in 2019. She stopped using the platform last year when she noticed competition for shifts growing—and pay rates declining.

“People were fighting over trash shifts for under $20 an hour,” noted Teresa, a single mother of three kids.

Smith remembers being able to bid $3 to $4 more an hour above the facility’s suggested rate when she first joined, but this year she said she’s been forced to accept less money or risk no work at all.

Recent findings suggest that according to her ShiftKey payment records that she shared with Proof News and Wired, one facility paid her $32.50 an hour in the summer of 2025 and around $26 a year later. Payments from another nursing home demonstrated the same downward trend. On Facebook groups, many ShiftKey workers have posted about a similar dip in earnings.

It has been revealed that “The starting bids are shamefully low,” mentioned Smith. “It’s not worth the workload or the drive.”.

It has been revealed that during her four years with ShiftKey, Smith mentioned she routinely felt “thrown in” at newly introduced facilities without orientation, clear instructions, or logins. She said she had to work hard to familiarize herself with the residents’ conditions, because critical details, such as who is a fall risk or who has a catheter or an ostomy, are frequently missing. Hours in, she felt like she was in “an ocean and nobody’s around me.”.

Sources indicate that “We're coming there because they're short-handed,” noted Smith. “So we are automatically going to be walking into a shit show.”.

Recent findings suggest that smith noted a lack of orientation led to scary close calls. Last year, she notes she arrived at a Virginia nursing home with no advance information, not even the door code. She didn’t know anything about the patients, and that made her “very stressed out.”.

“I know my blood pressure went up because of it,” she noted.

Another time, Smith noted she dropped off a regular drink to a resident only to later learn that they were prescribed only thickened liquids to avoid choking.

“What if they choked and died?” mentioned Smith.

In a recent development, facilities on ShiftKey have the option to require that workers attend a paid “orientation shift” before picking up a regular one. But four ShiftKey workers told Proof News and WIRED that they've frequently picked up nursing home shifts without doing an orientation shift first.

Inspection reports from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services dating back to 2023 and obtained by Proof News and WIRED reveal ShiftKey workers making dangerous mistakes.

In Ohio, after a ShiftKey nurse made a PICC line mistake at Stellar Care Center, a federal inspection report noted that the nursing home’s administrators had never checked to see whether she was trained to do IV therapy.

The report noted that an administrator had spoken with someone at ShiftKey, who told her that because they consider everyone on the app an independent contractor, the company didn’t test for what skills they knew.

In other cases, the orientation was inadequate. At Woodway Rehabilitation and Healthcare Center in Texas, a federal health surveyor spotted a ShiftKey worker trying to force-feed a resident a health shake using an oral syringe. The ShiftKey worker noted it was her first time at the facility, according to the 2025 inspection report. She received some orientation for the facility on the app before she started her shift, the report said, but couldn’t remember if feeding was included.

In 2024, another CMS surveyor wrote that a ShiftKey nurse at the Medical Suites at Oak Creek in Wisconsin told the surveyor she was not shown any care aims for residents on her first day. According to the report, the surveyor spoke with an administrator, who handed the surveyor an undated orientation checklist. The administrator remarked they did not at the moment have a policy regarding orientation for gig nurses, but that she'd be implementing one in 30 minutes.

Neither Stellar Care, Woodway Rehab, nor the Medical Suites at Oak Creek responded to requests for comment on this story.

Researchers warn that gig nurses who aren’t properly oriented and who move constantly between facilities can disrupt the continuity of care. Jasmine Travers Altizer, an assistant professor at Fresh York University’s Rory Meyers College of Nursing, conducted a qualitative study of 22 nursing home administrators this year and found that they felt relying on temporary workers led to “less consistent care, more hospital transfers, potentially unnecessary treatments and antibiotic use, and increased falls.” Administrators also reported staff having less ability to support one another across the facility.

Gig nursing “shouldn't be a fix for chronic understaffing,” said Travers Altizer in an email. It's critical, she said, to “have consistent staff who know the residents.”.

In response, Vitek, the ShiftKey CEO, stated, “Continuity of care is an notable consideration in nursing home quality, but the issue predates platforms like ours.”.

ShiftKey claims its model keeps more nurses on the job during a time of critical shortage. Vitek said a survey of workers on ShiftKey found that more than a third stated they would not be able to stay in the health care industry without such a platform.

“We reject the premise that enabling independent flexible nursing support is harmful to the industry, because the challenge in addressing these complications is not about the choice between full-time staff versus temporary shift support,” he said.

It has been revealed that katie Wells, a researcher who tracks gig nursing, said a combination of factors made platforms like ShiftKey an attractive option for nursing homes. Health care facilities were struggling financially, and many of them had been taken over by private equity, which Wells said “contributed to lean staffing models that make facilities more likely to want to just plug the hole rather than invest in a larger staff.”.

According to recent reports, according to CMS data, the average time worked by nursing staff per resident at Peachtree, where Lewis was accidentally injected, is lower than the state average and less than minimum requirements set by the US Department of Health and Human Services under the Biden administration that are no longer in effect. The American Health Care Association, a nonprofit group that represents nursing homes, successfully challenged the rule in court in 2025, and the Trump administration ultimately withdrew the rule, stating that the move would save nursing homes $55.1 billion over the course of 10 years.

It has been revealed that “We need to have minimum safe staffing levels,” stated Hannah Garden-Monheit, who worked on nursing home reform at the White House National Economic Council and now is executive director of Columbia Law School’s Center for Law and the Economy. “The patients need that continuity of care.”.

Half a dozen ShiftKey nurses and the two former corporate employees told Proof News and WIRED that many of the facilities that use ShiftKey have a history of poor quality of care and staffing issues.

One ShiftKey nurse recalled rats scurrying in the ceiling and roaches falling from lights at one nursing home.

Constance Hicks, a longtime certified nursing assistant in Connecticut, said that most nursing homes she worked at through ShiftKey were in terrible condition: no barrier cream, no soap, no supplies. Some places had no hot water. Not once in more than a year of picking up shifts through ShiftKey does she remember receiving any training at the homes.

In November 2023, while working a double shift at Cobalt Lodge Healthcare, Hicks discovered an elderly patient with their head and neck trapped in a bed rail, their forehead compressed against the metal, according to court records. She checked the patient’s vitals and, finding dangerously high blood pressure, called 911. Even though her shift had ended, Hicks stayed until emergency workers arrived.

Hicks noted she documented everything and sent it to ShiftKey. She also tried reaching out to the firm’s representatives but said no one responded. By the next day, her ShiftKey account was deactivated.

Hicks, who says the incident with the patient caused “a whole lot of psychological trauma,” tried to file a lawsuit against ShiftKey over the deactivation and other issues, but court records show the firm successfully moved her case to private arbitration.

Cobalt Lodge Healthcare did not respond to a request for comment, and ShiftKey declined, citing ongoing litigation.

Regarding the quality of the facilities, Vitek said, “When professionals raise a concern, we encourage them to use the formal reporting channels, and remind them that they can choose whether they can accept future shifts there.”.

Some lawmakers have begun scrutinizing platforms like ShiftKey, in part over concerns that it’s misclassifying its workers as independent contractors.

A gig nurse logs into ShiftKey.

Sources indicate that “It's not like they're coming in, bringing their own tools, fixing a pipe, and leaving,” notes Emma Greenman, a Minnesota state representative, of gig nurses. “They are being managed by somebody.”.

According to recent reports, shiftKey disputes that characterization. “ShiftKey, as a technology marketplace, does not employ healthcare professionals but connects them with healthcare facilities that have gaps in their schedule,” remarked Vitek, adding that the firm works “tirelessly” to ensure its model complies with the law.

Greenman is working on a bill that she noted would curb worker misclassification in Minnesota, including in gig nursing.

“What they’re doing is building business models to evade, break, and distort labor law for profit,” Greenman said.

It has been revealed that there’s also the issue of whether to allow nursing homes to staff largely with gig workers. The year Lewis died, an analysis of staffing data submitted to CMS reveals that nearly a third of the total nursing staff hours at Peachtree were performed by temporary workers.

Gary Poliakoff, one of the attorneys representing Lewis’ family, said that some weeks, the rate of temp workers including ShiftKey rose to as high as 50 percent of all nursing staff.

With little orientation, Poliakoff said, the model puts both patients—and workers—at a “great disadvantage.”.

According to recent reports, after the mistaken insulin injection, James Lewis remarked he got the call from Peachtree letting him know his mother was in the hospital. According to his deposition, he was getting ready to go to church to preach and planned to visit her later. He often went every day. They’d eat lunch together and watch The Price Is Right, but that day he was looking forward to spending some time outside. It was Mother’s Day.

When asked if he knew that Peachtree sometimes had temporary workers, he responded that he wasn’t aware.

Recent findings suggest that “I don't know if it was a traveling nurse or what,” he noted in the deposition. “But I know it wasn't a regular person.”.

In her testimony, Kaye blamed understaffing for her insulin mix-up. She remembered working at Peachtree twice in November 2021 but went six months without returning because she thought it was a “shithole.”.

“It was not a nice facility by any means,” Kaye mentioned.

She testified she was already an hour late giving the insulin, having too much on her plate.

“I remember being not helped at all by administration, not knowing who anyone was,” noted Kaye. “And pretty much being by myself.”.
